summary: A German adjective has two lives. After sein (and werden, bleiben) and as an adverb it never changes: Das Haus ist groß. Der Zug fährt schnell. Before a noun it always takes an ending, and the ending depends on the word in front of it. The rule of thumb: the article and the adjective share the job of showing gender and case – if the article already shows it clearly (der, die, das, dem, den, dieser …), the adjective only adds the weak ending -e or -en; if there is no article, or the article has no ending (ein, kein, mein in the masculine nominative and the neuter nominative/accusative), the adjective takes the strong ending that der/das would have had (-er, -es). The WEAK endings are learned in one sentence: -e in the five “light” places (nominative singular of all three genders, accusative singular feminine and neuter), -en everywhere else – all datives and all plurals included. German puts the adjective before the noun (Arabic and Hebrew put it after). Feelings of the body use the dative or haben, not sein + adjective: Mir ist kalt (I’m cold), Ich habe Hunger / Durst (I’m hungry / thirsty).

blocks.title: One question decides
blocks.text: Does the word in front already show the gender and case with its own ending? Yes (der, dem, den, dieser, meinem …) → the adjective is weak: -e or -en. No (ein, kein, mein with no ending; no article at all) → the adjective shows it: -er (der), -es (das), -e (die), -em (dem), -en (den).

blocks.title: mein großer Bruder
blocks.text: groß and klein before family words mean older and younger: mein großer Bruder (my older brother), meine kleine Schwester (my little sister).

blocks.title: Ask yourself before an adjective
questions: Is it after sein / werden / bleiben, or does it describe a verb? → no ending.
Is there a word in front of it? Which one?
Does that word show gender and case with its own ending (der, dem, den, dieser, meinem …)? → weak: -e or -en.
Is it ein / kein / mein without an ending (masculine nominative, neuter nominative/accusative)? → -er (masc.) or -es (neuter).
No article at all (or a number, viele)? → strong: the ending of der / die / das: -er, -e, -es, -en, -em.
Dative or plural after an article? → -en.
Does the stem change? hoch → hoh-, teuer → teur-, dunkel → dunkl-; rosa, lila, orange never change.

askYourself: Is the adjective after sein / werden / bleiben, or used as an adverb? → no ending.
Which word stands in front of it: der-word, ein-word, or nothing?
Does the determiner show the case and gender itself (der, die, das, dem, den, dieser, meinem …)? → weak: -e / -en.
ein, kein, mein … with no ending (masc. nominative, neuter nominative/accusative)? → -er / -es on the adjective.
No determiner (or a number, viele, einige)? → strong: -er, -e, -es, -en, -em like the article.
Is the noun dative, or plural after an article? → -en.
Does the stem change (hoh-, teur-, dunkl-, müd-), or is it an invariant colour (rosa, lila, orange)?
Is it a feeling of the body? → Mir ist kalt / heiß; Ich habe Hunger / Durst.
steps: Find the noun and its gender, number and case.
Look at the determiner in front of the adjective.
Pick weak, mixed or strong and add the ending.

traps: Before a noun there is always an ending: *ein groß Haus is wrong – ein großes Haus.
After sein no ending: Das Haus ist groß (not *ist großes).
ein + masculine nominative → -er: ein großer Tisch (not *ein große Tisch).
Dative after an article is always -en: mit dem neuen Auto, in einer kleinen Wohnung.
Plural after die / keine / meine → -en; after numbers and viele → -e: zwei kleine Kinder.
hoch → ein hohes Haus (not *hoches); teuer → ein teures Auto; dunkel → ein dunkles Bier.
Tall of people is groß, not hoch.
Mir ist kalt (I’m cold), not *Ich bin kalt; Ich habe Hunger is the usual “I’m hungry”.
The adverb is the bare adjective: Er fährt schnell (fast / quickly).

quiz.why: ein has no ending in the neuter → the adjective shows it: -es.
der already shows masculine nominative → weak -e.
No article, masculine accusative → strong -en (like den).
hoch loses its c before an ending: hoh-.
A number is not an article → strong plural -e.
People are groß; hoch is for buildings and mountains.
Bodily feelings take the dative: mir ist kalt. Ich bin kalt = I’m cold-hearted.
German “has” hunger; Ich bin hungrig is correct but less common.
teuer drops the e before r: teur-.

seeAlso.note: Arabic puts the adjective AFTER the noun and makes it agree in gender, number, case and definiteness: بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ (a big house), الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ (the big house) – the article is repeated.
Hebrew also puts it after the noun, agreeing in gender and number, with הַ repeated when the noun is definite: בַּיִת גָּדוֹל, הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל.
Chinese adjectives are stative verbs: no 是, usually 很 in a statement (房子很大); before a noun with 的 (很大的房子) or directly for short ones (大房子). No endings at all.
The endings of der / ein from S04 are the model of the strong and mixed endings here.
The case after a preposition decides the adjective ending too: mit dem neuen Auto (dative), für den kleinen Jungen (accusative).

notes.text: A Greek adjective agrees with its noun whatever stands before it, also after είναι (το σπίτι είναι μεγάλο); German endings depend on the article (der große / ein großer) and disappear after sein: Das Haus ist groß.
Russian adjectives agree in gender, number and case, as German ones do, but their ending does not depend on the article (Russian has none); German has weak, mixed and strong endings.
Spanish puts most adjectives after the noun (una casa grande) and they always agree; German puts them before and changes them only there: ein großes Haus, but Das Haus ist groß.
English adjectives never change; German ones take an ending before the noun, chosen by the article. The adverb has no -ly: schnell = fast and quickly. “I’m cold” is Mir ist kalt.
Most French adjectives follow the noun and always agree (la maison est grande); German ones precede the noun and agree only there.

Hindi adjectives in -ā agree (achchhā laṛkā, achchhī laṛkī, achchhe laṛke) and come before the noun, as in German; others never change (sundar). mujhe ṭhaṇḍ lag rahī hai has the experiencer in the dative, like Mir ist kalt.
Persian adjectives follow the noun with the ezafe and never change (ketāb-e bozorg); German ones precede it and take endings: ein großes Buch.
Adjectives in -ā agree in gender and precede the noun, as in German; German adds case and the choice between weak and strong endings.
Arabic adjectives follow the noun and agree in gender, number, case and definiteness (al-baytu l-kabīru); German ones precede it, and the article decides the ending: das große Haus, ein großes Haus.
Hebrew adjectives follow the noun and repeat the article (ha-bayit ha-gadol); German ones precede the noun and take an ending: das große Haus.
Turkish adjectives never change (büyük ev, büyük evler); German ones do, before a noun. “I’m cold” is a verb in Turkish (üşüyorum), a dative phrase in German: Mir ist kalt.
Japanese i-adjectives inflect for tense like verbs (takai, takakatta); German adjectives have no tense, but take case and gender endings before a noun.
Korean adjectives are verbs (keuda, keun jip); a German adjective needs sein as a predicate and an ending before a noun.
Finnish adjectives agree in case and number before the noun (isossa talossa), as German ones do – but without gender, and without the weak / strong choice.
Hungarian attributive adjectives never change (a nagy házban); German ones always take an ending before a noun: in dem großen Haus.
Swahili adjectives follow the noun and agree by class (kitabu kikubwa, vitabu vikubwa); German ones precede the noun and agree by gender, number and case.
Chinese adjectives precede the noun with or without 的 (大房子, 很大的房子) and never change; as a predicate they need no copula (房子很大). German needs sein (Das Haus ist groß) and endings before the noun.
Vietnamese adjectives follow the noun (nhà lớn) and need no copula (nhà lớn = the house is big); German puts them before the noun with an ending and uses sein in a predicate.
Inuktitut has no separate class of adjectives: a quality is a verb or a suffix on the noun (-rjuaq, big). German adjectives are words of their own, with endings before the noun.
